question:
Patient note:
A 44-year-old woman presented to the same-day assessment unit this afternoon complaining that her right lower leg had become visibly larger and “water-logged” over the prior twenty-four hours, making her shoe feel tighter and leaving deep sock imprints that persisted for minutes. She reports awakening yesterday with an ill-defined heaviness in the distal calf that progressed throughout the day despite elevating the leg on an ottoman while working remotely; by this morning she noted a shiny fullness around the ankle and felt a dull ache when standing to prepare breakfast. She denies antecedent trauma, sprains, insect bites, rashes, fever, or chills and has experienced no chest pain, cough, dyspnea, palpitations, syncope, flank discomfort, abdominal pain, or urinary symptoms. Three years ago she developed an acute proximal left-leg venous thrombosis postpartum, treated with six months of rivaroxaban, after which follow-up duplex studies were normal and anticoagulation was discontinued. Gynecologic review notes an uncomplicated total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingectomy performed seven weeks ago for symptomatic fibroids; the operation required a midline laparotomy and a two-night hospital stay but no transfusion, and she resumed light walking within a week. She has not been bedridden since discharge, has no limb casts, splints, or braces, ambulates independently, and performs brief household tasks without assistance. Medical history is otherwise significant only for seasonal allergic rhinitis; she takes fexofenadine daily, an over-the-counter vitamin D supplement, and combined medication-free contraception is no longer needed after surgery. She has never used estrogen replacement, glucocorticoids, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or chemotherapy, and there is no family history of malignancy or inherited thrombophilia. She quit smoking ten years ago after a five-pack-year exposure, drinks a glass of wine on weekends, and denies recreational drug use. On arrival—prior to any analgesics, intravenous fluids, or anticoagulants—she sat comfortably with the right leg elevated on the stretcher rail. Vital signs recorded temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 118/76 mm Hg, heart rate 88 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 99 % breathing ambient air. Neck veins were flat, heart tones were crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs or gallops, and lungs were clear throughout. The abdominal incision was well-healed, non-tender, and showed no hernia or seroma. Inspection of the lower extremities revealed mild circumferential swelling extending from just above the medial malleolus to mid-calf on the right; the overlying skin was taut and glossy yet maintained normal pink coloration with intact hair growth. A thumb pressed firmly over the anterior tibial crest of the right leg for ten seconds produced a 4-mm depression that lingered for approximately twenty seconds, whereas identical pressure on the contralateral side rebounded immediately. Circumferential measurement taken 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity measured 37.0 cm on the right and 33.5 cm on the left (difference 3.5 cm). No tortuous subcutaneous venous channels, varicosities, ulcerations, brawny discoloration, or stasis dermatitis were seen on either limb, nor were any engorged superficial veins coursing over the thigh or calf suggestive of collateralization observed. Palpation of the inguinal ligament, femoral triangle, adductor canal, popliteal fossa, posterior tibial track, and peroneal compartment elicited diffuse fullness but no discrete cord or focal tenderness; compressing the gastrocnemius belly caused only a dull, non-localized ache. Passive ankle dorsiflexion reproduced a stretching sensation but not sharp pain. Hip, knee, and ankle ranges of motion were full and painless, distal sensation was intact to light touch and vibration, and motor strength graded 5/5 throughout both legs. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were 2+ and symmetric, and capillary refill to all toes was under two seconds. No inguinal or popliteal lymphadenopathy, crepitus, fluctuance, or calf firmness suggestive of compartment syndrome was detected, and there was no lymphedema elsewhere. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained before phlebotomy revealed normal sinus rhythm at 86 beats/min without ST-T abnormalities. Baseline laboratory studies drawn prior to any therapy showed hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, white blood cells 7.1 × 10⁹/L, platelets 243 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 11 mg/dL, creatinine 0.87 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 21 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 19 U/L, international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 28 s. A supine anteroposterior chest radiograph displayed clear lung fields and normal cardiac silhouette. Radiographs of the tibia and fibula obtained earlier at her primary clinic showed only soft-tissue prominence without bony lesion. No cellulitis, ruptured Baker cyst, Achilles tendinopathy, heart failure signs, renal disease, or systemic inflammatory condition offers a more convincing explanation for her new unilateral pitting edema emerging seven weeks after major pelvic surgery in a patient with prior venous thrombosis, so comprehensive duplex ultrasonography from the common femoral vein to the calf veins has been ordered while she remains hemodynamically stable and untreated in observation with the limb elevated.

Question: What is the patient's score of Wells' criteria for Deep Vein Thrombosis? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Wells DVT score adds 1 per positive clinical criterion and subtracts 2 if an alternative diagnosis is at least as likely as DVT. The surgery lookback matters here.
At presentation, prior documented DVT scores 1; calf asymmetry ≥3 cm scores 1 (37.0 − 33.5 = 3.5 cm at the specified measurement site); and pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg scores 1.
Active cancer, leg paralysis/paresis or cast immobilization, localized deep venous tenderness, entire-leg swelling, and nonvaricose collateral veins each score 0. No alternative diagnosis is at least as likely, so there is no deduction.
Using a 4-week surgery window, the operation 7 weeks ago does not qualify, and she was not bedridden for ≥3 days: 0. Sum = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. With the commonly used modified Wells 12-week window, the major surgery adds 1 and the score is 4 instead.
Final answer: 3
